Dear Editor,

I am submitting "Testing the wind disruption hypothesis for beetle refugia" for
consideration as an Original Article in *Journal of Applied Entomology*.

Krawchuk et al. (2020) proposed that refugia from mountain pine beetle (*Dendroctonus
ponderosae* Hopkins) could arise through three mechanisms: topographic shading that
relieves water stress, low host density that admits wind and so disrupts the aggregation
pheromone plume on which mass attack depends, and a scarcity of large-diameter hosts.
That proposal is now widely cited and, so far as a search of the author's full corpus can
establish, it has never been fitted. This paper fits all three on one landscape.

The central result is that the wind mechanism holds, but only when the response is
measured at a resolution the insect can be said to experience. Across 59 sixteen-day
Landsat epochs, stand density interacts negatively with a terrain-resolved wind field:
a dense canopy is worth less to the beetle where and when the wind blows harder, which is
what plume disruption requires. The interaction survives a within-season spread term, so
it is not the outbreak's own contagion wearing a wind coefficient.

The finding I expect to be most useful to your readers concerns what a beetle refugium is.
Wind has no main effect on attack in these models. What it does is change what stand
density is worth. A refugium from beetle is therefore not a place on a map but a
conjunction: a thin stand and wind, in the same weeks the insect flies. A manager mapping exposed ground will
find nothing, and so will one mapping thin stands.

The failure of the shading mechanism points the same way. It does not merely fail to
reach significance; it runs backwards, with shaded ground carrying more attack than
exposed ground, not less. The most intuitive piece of the fire framework, that cool
ground protects trees, is the piece that fails hardest here.

Two measurement results bear on any study of this kind. Entering flight-window
radiation cuts the apparent density-by-terrain-exposure interaction by about two fifths, so a
terrain wind index is partly an insolation measurement. Entering previous-year attack
destabilises the landform terms, so a landform variable in a spreading outbreak partly
records where the outbreak has already been.

The manuscript is an executable Quarto document. Every number, table and figure in it is
computed at render time from the archived data, and no value is typed into the prose. The
complete pipeline is public.

This work is original, has not been published elsewhere and is not under consideration by
another journal. I am the sole author. I declare no conflict of interest, and the work
received no external funding.

Yours sincerely,

Seamus Murphy
